RELATIVE TO OUR PEOPLE THE COUNTRY OVER. Interesting Items In Condensed Form Culled From Exchanges for the Perusal of The Gazette Readers.
Judge Okey, of the Ohio Supreme bench died at Columbus, July 25.

Reports are adrift that El Mahdi fell ill on June 19, and died on June 22.

A Negro named Peter Stamps was taken from the jail at Douglassville, Ga., and lynched for outraging a little white girl.

It was the proprietor of a hotel at Pierce City, and not Prince City, Mo., which Hon. J. Milton Turner is reported to have sued for $50,000 for refusing him accommodations.

Fred Williams and Joe Turkington, Springfield colored boys, played in the woods Friday with a knife. Fred dared Joe to throw the knife at him. Joe did so, and Fred now has a fatal wound near the heart.

Colonel W. A. Pledger, having resigned his position as Surveyor of Customs of Atlanta, will retire to Athens, Ga., his home, and will in consequence sever his connection with the Weekly Defiance, the bravest paper of its kind in the South.

The Democratic Police Board, of Cincinnati, appointed Mr. Carroll as special policeman of the Cincinnati force. Mr. Carroll is the first colored man to receive such an appointment at the hands of a Democratic Board in Cincinnati.

Allen O. Myers says, referring to the Governor's respite of Murderer Griener, that if "Hoadly had been Governor of Judea in place of Pontius Pilate he would undoubtedly have postponed the crucifixion until after the fall election, and thus deprived the world of the Christian religion."

Lucien Lee, Dayton colored man, dreamed for three nights in succession that he had found a box of money under a flat stone on the Stillwater River. Was so impressed on his mind that he searched the river bank and actually found the box, he claims. It contained $752.50, which he banked. Lucien has a good reputation.

A fine Masonic flower emblem has been presented by Hon. E. P. McCabe, State Auditor of Kansas, to the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of Kansas. This emblem beautifully represents the Lodge of K. T., Chapter and Blue Lodge, and surpasses anything of the kind ever presented in the State.

There are probably a dozen colored men in New Orleans worth over $100,-000 in real estate, most of whom inherited their wealth, were always rich, and never fought their way up from slavery. A few weeks ago the Christ Church property on Canal street, the seat of the first Protestant church in the Mississippi Valley, was purchased by the Mercier Brothers for $95,000. They are now erecting upon it the finest business block in the city. It will cost over $120,000. The Merciers, who control perhaps the largest clothing business in New Orleans, and who have a hundred or more white men in their employ, are colored—true representatives of the old free people of color of New Orleans. Opposite the custom house is another row of elegant commercial buildings, also the property of a colored man, Aristides Marie, as fine a type of the colored aristocrat as one would want to see—elegant in his dress and manners, a type of a fine French gentleman.

I. L. Milan, passenger agent of the East Tennessee, Virginia & Georgia Railway, went to Waterloo County, S. C., to obtain transportation for six colored women to Arkansas. On his arrival he was advised by several to leave the place, as the white people of the county had threatened to kill the first one who attempted to induce the Negroes to leave. A short time afterwards a mob arrived at the hotel at which Mr. Milan was stopping, carried him some distance from the hotel, whipped him most brutally and compelled him to walk several miles through the woods. As they left him they advised him never again to attempt to persuade the Negroes of that vicinity to leave. In the consideration of labor the Negroes seem to be of extreme importance to the Southern whites. To their social worth and mental qualifications the Southern whites attach no importance.

LACK OF LAW IN LAURENS. AN INVESTIGATION OF THE RECENT OUTRAGES. A Negro Murdered by a Negro---A Suspicious Lynching--Public Opinion in Laurens C. H., Forces the Resignation of the Intendant and Wardens on Account of the Irby Case --- Milam more Scarrd than Hurt --- The Dastardly Assassination of Warren Bennett---What the People of Laurens Think about the Outrages --- The Inefficient Character of the Officers of the Law. THE NEWS AND COURTER BUREAU OAKLAND, CALIFORNIA JULY 20
On the 19th of July Alfred Dean, alias Alfred Harley, colored, shot and killed Mack Byrd, also colored. The next day Coroner Job J. Boozer held an inquest, the evidence taken being fled in the office of the Clerk of Court on July 28. The murderer had fled, but the Governor had not been notified of the result of the inquest or of the flight until the 30th of July. There was nothing remarkable about this case, and I did not investigate it further.

A Peculiar Lynching.

On the night of the Fourth of July Charles Williams, colored, who had been arrested for an alleged attempt to ravish a young white girl, was being conveyed under guard to Laurens Court House, when he was taken from the constables and shot to death in the public road, about five and a half miles from Laurens Court House. The inquest was held on the 5th inst. by Trial Justice W. B. Toddard, acting coroner, but the evidence was only filed with the Clerk of the Court on the 27th, and no report has been made to the Governor.

The evidence recorded is very brief and covers only the testimony of Constable J. A. Burdett, his assistant, Eddie Shell, and J. A. Rodgers, who found the dead body in the road. The evidence of the two first was to the effect that they were leading Williams by the rope with which he was bound; that he complained that he could hardly travel on account of the beating he had received that morning; that while he was going along and assseverating his innocence his conductors were halted by twelve or fifteen men, whose color they did not discern, although no mention of masks is recorded; that these men helped themselves to the prisoner, while he protested his innocence, and took him down the road, and that his late keepers heard shots fired and went on to Laurens. There is no mention of any resistance on the part of either guard or prisoner. Mr. Rodgers testified to finding the negro in the road shot through the head. An account of this lynching from one standpoint has already appeared in the News and Courier. The negro was stated to have been identified as one who entered the room on a young girl at night and placed his hand upon her head, but who, alarmed by her outcry, retreated precipitately. I have been informed of another side of the story. It is alleged by persons acquainted with the family that three elder sisters of the girl were of loose character, and surmised that the negro mistook her for one of them. The inference is a horrible one, but it belongs to the case and cannot be ignored.

Comment.—Lynching as a punishment for attempts upon female honor is an established and approved practice in South Carolina; but the scent evidence in this case and the soffo voice talk which one hears impress me with the opinion that there should be a more searching investigation of the facts.

The Irby Case.

The News and Courier has already published in full the Laurensville Herald's statement of both sides of the Irby matter, and it is unnecessary for me to repeat the details. It is admitted that Mr. Palmer and Col. J. L. M. Irby had words as to their relative muscle; that Col. Irby told Palmer that he declined to put himself on a level with him, but that he would furnish a man who would whip him; that he brought his negro servant, San Chapell, to town stood by with a pistol while the negro battered Palmer with his fists; that he admitted his violation of the town ordinance and expressed his willingness to be tried; that he heard that Mr. J. J. Pluss had spoken disparagingly of him, and got intoxicated on the strength of it; that he armed himself with a Winchester rifle and revolver, paraded the public square cursing and threatening his supposed enemies; that he sought Mr. Pluss and lunged at him with the muzzle of his rifle; that Mr. Pluss caught it and wrenched it from him and that he then drow his revolver and was disarmed of that also; that Mr. Pluss and Col. Irby's brother bore him to the ground and that Mr. Pluss choked him a little to subdue him, and held him down until he was taken to a carriage and conveyed to his home several miles from the town; that when sober he returned to town and readily gave two bonds for five hundred dollars each—one for assault with intent to kill and the other a peace bond—both being the result of warcouts sworn out by Mr. Pluss.

Col. Irby expressed a desire to see me and talked freely, moderately and courteously on the subject. He admitted, he said, that it was not lawful for him to knock people about, or to get a substitute to do it, but he thought that in the case of Palmer it was excusable on account of the character of the man. Palmer had made himself very obnoxious to gentlemen and was constantly embroiled. He had insulted him and dared a fight and he had selected a negro of about his size and put him to the test. His relations with Mr. Pluss had been very friendly and he had naught against him. He did not remember anything about his assault on him for he was intoxicated.

He did not admit, however, that he had in any degree sought to kill him. He desired to say that he condemned lawlessness as heartily as any man. He had himself broken the law, but he did not shirk the consequences.

"Whiskey," I suggested, "was at the bottom of the whole affair?"

"Yes" was the reply, "you are about right."

I interviewed Mr. Pluss, who is a member of a large mercantile firm, and has an excellent standing in the community. He said that Col. Irby when sober was entirely inoffensive and courteous, but when intoxicated was almost crazy. He had no feeling against him, but he had sworn out the warrants from a sense of public duty. It was a disgrace to the town that a man should be permitted to go armed about the streets, threatening and cursing and assaulting without hindrance by the authorities. He wisened the law vindicated and turbulence suppressed, once for all. He could have taken Col. Irby's own gun or pistol and killed him, but he declined to take advantage of what would have been his legal right. He intended only to bring him face to face with the law.

Mr. Palmer is not favorably regarded in Laurens. He is a Canadian, a painter by trade, and has been in the town only a few months. It is said in all quarters that he is frequently intoxicated, and that when so he is insolent to people who have said nothing to him and seeks quarrels and street fights.

Col. Irby is said to be a veritable madman when intoxicated, but at other times quiet and courteous. As to the action of the officials, Sheriff Ballew denied point blank that he was present when either assault occurred. He was the one who arrested Col. Irby at his home.

Mr. Charles Myers, the town marshal, (and the only local peace officer) is said to be a determined man. It is stated that he went to the acting intendant, Mr. F. Robertson, and asked him if he should arrest Col. Irby. The intendant was indifferent and said that he "night as well let the thing go!" At this reply the marshal pulled off his badge, put down his club and resigned. In view of the resignation of the intendant and council he was afterwards induced to serve until a new council should be elected. It is believed that he would have made the arrest promptly if authorized to do so.

The people of the town whom I talked to criticised the management of the affair very freely. Considering

Lawlessness in Laurens. [News and (survey]
The special correspondent of the News and Courier who was sent to Laurens County a few days ago to investigate the several instances of lawlessness which have recently occurred in that county has performed the duty assigned to him, and reports, the result in a letter which we published to-day.

The inquiries of our correspondent were conducted in a careful and impartial spirit, with no other purpose than to elicit the truth, and as the information which he obtained was derived from the most trustworthy sources, there can be no question as to its substantial accuracy. It shows, moreover, that the accounts of the lawlessness in Laurens County which have already been published in the News and Courier and in the Laurensville Herald have not exaggerated either the nature of the crimes or the indifference and neglect displayed by the local authorities in failing to discharge their duty with reference to the criminals.

It is not necessary to repeat the details that have been given in regard to the assaults instigated and committed by Col. Irby upon Palmer and Pluss, respectively. There were numerous witnesses of these assaults, and both will be made the subject of a judicial investigation, the results of which may not properly be anticipated. Col. Irby is under bond to answer to the serious charges made against him, and the people of Laurens must now look to their Courts to assert and vindicate the law which he admits that he has violated. It is stated that Col. Irby is a courteous gentleman and good citizen when not under the influence of liquor, and no one should know better than himself the gravity of his offence and the necessity for its punishment. When men of his character and standing give way to violent passion and imperil the lives of their fellow-men with impunity, under whatever circumstances, it is not surprising that their example should be followed by men of lower class, who are without the restraining influence of education, personal pride and social position, and that lawlessness should prevail among them to any extent.

There is nothing to be said save in the way of strong condemnation in regard to the lynching of the negro Charles Williams, and the deliberate and hastily murder of the colored boy Warren Bennett. In the case of Williams the victim was taken from the custody of the officers of the law while carnestly protesting his innocence, and was shot dead in the public highway by the self-appointed jury and executioners. There is no hint that even a form of irregular trial was had in this case and the victim was apparently sacrifice.
in the public highway by the self-appointed jury and executioners. There is no hint that even a form of irregular trial was had in this case, and the victim was apparently sacrificed to the blind rage of his murderers, without an effort on their part to established the fact of his guilt.

In the other case, that of the killing of Bennett, the testimony so far obtained shows that the murder was one of the most atrocious crimes ever committed in this State. It should have been promptly investigated, and the delay that has already occurred in its investigation casts a deep reproach upon the responsible officials of the county. The testimony of a number of persons points clearly to one or both of two men as being concerned in the murder; their names and the circumstances which indicate their guilt are generally known and discussed in the county, but no effort was made to arrest them until sufficient time had elapsed to allow them to escape.

The story of the alleged ill treatment of the emigration agent, Milam, which was first published in an Atlanta paper, appears to have been greatly exaggerated. The truth in regard to this occurrence is, apparently, that Milam became frightened in view of the threatening demonstrations made against him and fled the county without waiting for hostilities to begin. The pistol salute which hastened his sudden departure will suggest to many persons, however, that Milam did not leave too soon for his own comfort and safety.

Our correspondent was assured, and found reason to believe, that public sentiment in Laurens County is strongly opposed to the condition of affairs which provails there, and that the law abiding people of the county appreciate the injury that must result to them if the impression obtains abroad that the county is not a safe place to live in. It is very significant, however, that the colored people of the county have so far adsorbed that impression that large numbers of them have already moved away, and that it is necessary to banish emigration agents at the point of the pistol. It is time for the law-abiding citizens to declare and enforce their sentiments when colored laborers are afraid to work in the fields alone, and when white men are afraid to testify to crimes of which they have knowledge.

In view of the facts which are presented in the letter of our correspondent it will scarcely be disputed that a state of things exists in Laurens County that should be speedily remedied. The crimes enumerated are assuredly of a character to demand the promptest and most determined action on the part of the officers of the law, but such action has
medied. The crimes enumerated are assuredly of a character to demand the promptest and most determined action on the part of the officers of the law, but such action has not been had in any instance, so far as known. Even the plainest and simplest requirements of the criminal statutes have been disregarded, and official reports of brutal murders have been pigcon-hoiled for weeks, instead of being forwarded to the State authorities for the attention they required, and which was necessary to promote the ends of justice.

The people of Laurens County are said to be fully alive to the evils described and to the necessity of a change for the better. This is well, but it is not enough. Mere sentiment will accomplish nothing unless it is expressed and enforced. The root of the trouble manifestly lies in the inefficiency of the local authorities, and the work of reform must begin with them. The people of the county owe it to themselves and to the State to turn out the men who misrepresent them in public office, and who hold so lax views of their duties. A great deal has been accomplished in fixing the blame where it belongs, and the citizens of Laurens and Governor Thompson will not fail to do the rest.

Philadelphia Notes. Emancipation day was not forgotten at the Home for Aged and Infirm Colored Persons. It has been the custom for the late Mrs. Mary M. Johnson to furnish on this day ice cream and cake. To-day, although the large flag outside was draped for the late General Grant, inside the house was made bright by flowers and bunting, and on this occasion more so, as a large two-horse wagon containing 33 children, all inmates from the Home for Destitute Colored Children, arrived and marched into the room singing, with flags. Addresses were made by E. H. Cates, Mrs. F. W. Harper, Mrs. Fanny Coppin; recitations by Miss Harper, Mrs. McDowell and Mr. Strange. Music by Mrs. McMurtru, Mrs. Haas and son. After a bountiful repast of cream and cake the children returned home. All expressed themselves as having had a feast of good things. RUFFIAN BRUTALITY. The Mob Prevents Colored People from Leaving.
ATLANTA, Ga., July 25.—J. L. Milam, passenger agent of the East Tennessee, Virginia & Georgia Railway, went to Waterloo, Laurens County, S. C., to obtain transportation for six Negro women to Arkansas, where they were to meet their husbands. Arriving at the place, one of the women for whom he had transportation came to him and said that the white people were against the Negroes leaving that section; and furthermore that they had threatened to kill the first Negro who attempted to leave the place. Later, Mr. Perk, depot agent, advised him to leave, as the people there had threatened to kill the first person who attempted to buy transportation for Negroes. A few minutes after this conversation three men came into the hotel and called the proprietor into the yard. In a few minutes the proprietor returned and called Milam, and told him he had better go away, and that at once, showing him out the back gate, which led him into a large swamp. He had scarcely left the hotel when the proprietor gave a loud yell, which brought the mob in pursuit of him. About twenty shots were fired at him, the mob yelling at the same time "kill him, kill him!" The mob finally came up to him, tied his hands and beat him unmercifully. After doing this they made him walk four hours alongside of their horses through the woods and finally left him, with threats that if he ever came into that portion of the country that he would be instantly killed. Walking through the woods the greater part of the night Mr. Milam fainted from sheer exhaustion. He was picked up in the woods by a farmer and driven to the nearest station, where he boarded a train for Atlanta. He has arrived here and is yet in a serious condition from his treatment.

"It is about time that our people were putting a stop to that Southern deviltry. The only way to fight the devil successfully is to fight him with fire. The only right left the colored men in some parts of the South is the right to run away, and it seems that that right will soon be taken away from them. If our people will do their duty in that section of the country, they will arm themselves as best they can and the first colored man that is killed because he wants to take his family away from that place, let them turn out and kill every man that had any hand in killing that colored man. If they love their families they had better die fighting like men trying to protect them, than to play the coward and be treated like brutes.

"They will never have any peace in that country until they go to work like men and fight for their rights, and convince the white people of the South that they will not be imposed upon by them any longer. A great many of them would be killed in the struggle, but it ought to be a pleasure for a man to die fighting in defense of his family and his people.

"Every colored journal in the United States ought to arouse the colored people of the South to protect themselves at all hazards. If they cannot live there in peace, let them make it such a hell on earth that no one else can stay there. Then the United States Government will give them five or six of those Southern States to themselves. It will have to come to that anyway, and the sooner the better."

THE HOSTILE INDIANS.

Indians of Geronimo's band were reported from different sources, between the 22nd and 26th July, to be in the border mountains of Arizona.

It appears that the killing of F. M. Peterson, sub-contractor and carrier of mail from Crittenden to Lochiel, on the 23rd inst., was the work of Indians. His body was found near the old Mowry mines pierced through by two bullets. The mail bag was cut and rifled, and the letters torn into bits. The harness was cut up and the horse stolen. Citizens followed the trail for two days, when it was taken up by Capt. Lawton and five scouts and followed toward the Huachucas across the upper part of San Rafael Ranch.

The latest news is a despatch from Fort Huachucas, Arizona, July 30, to Capt. Roberts, Fort Bowie, signed by Lieut. Col. Forsyth, commanding: Mr. Levis, one of the citizens who was with Captains Wood and Hatfield, left them on trail Tuesday, sixty miles in Mexico, just at the summit of the Covano Mountains. Trail hot and troops in full pursuit. In my opinion this band of ten or twelve Indians is the only one that has been on our side of the line, notwithstanding the other reports. They came up to steal stock, but have had to drop nearly all of it so far. Since Wood has been on their track they have dropped forty head, which citizens have picked up. Wood's scouts played out and came back. Fortunately Hatfield's were mounted and are with command. The lightning smashed our telephone yesterday and we have to send to siding for despatches.

MOB RULE IN THE SOUTH.

J. L. Milam, a railway passenger agent, went to Waterloo, South Carolina, recently, to obtain the transportation for six negro women to Arkansas, where they were to meet their husbands. On arriving, the women met him and told him they were afraid to talk with him, as the white folks had threatened to kill the first negro who attempted to leave the place. About an hour after this conversation a mob of sixty men was collected by a man named Casper Smith. Milam asked the mob what were their intentions,
and the only reply was thatanemigrant agent stood a bad show in that country. Mr. Pard, the depot agent, advised him to leave, as the people there had sworn to kill the first man who attempted to persuade the negroes to leave that country. A few minutes later the proprietor of the hotel was called out into the yard by three men, and on his return he warned Milam to leave at once, and showed him the way out, by a back gate leading to a cotton field and that to a swamp. He had scarcely left the hotel when the proprietor gave a loud yell, which brought the mob in pursuit of him. About twenty shots were fired at him, the mob yelling at the same time "Kill him! Kill him!" The mob finally came up with him, tied his hands and beat him unmercifully. After doing this they made him walk four hours alongside their horses through the woods, and finally left him with the threat that if he ever came into that portion of the country again he would be instantly killed. Before leaving they gave him a farewell reminder in the shape of several kicks and cuffs. After walking through the woods the greater part of the night Milam fainted from sheer exhaustion. He was picked up in the woods by a farmer and taken in a cart drawn by an old negro to the nearest station, where he boarded the train for Atlanta. He reached there in a serious condition from his wounds.

CONDENSED TELEGRAMS.
Over four hundred Hungarians and Polanders have left Hazleton, Pa., for the Northwest, and it is expected that a great many more will leave for the same region in a few days.

George Campbell, with numerous aliases, was arrested at Springfield, Ohio, Friday night, and taken to Nicholasville, Ky., to answer for the murder of Jesse Williams, committed two years ago.

Yellow fever is raging on the Pacific Coast of Mexico and has appeared both at Guayamas and Mazatian. Late reports from Vera Cruz say the scourge is continually spreading, notwithstanding the untiring efforts of the authorities.

James Merrill, a bridge carpenter on the C. & M. R. R., was instantly killed by a fall from a trestle near Cambridge, Ohio.

At Polk, O., Willie Moon, aged 9 years, shot his sister Jennie, aged 6, with his father's musket, killing her instantly.

Freddie Doran, a two year old boy, fell from the second-story platform of a Cincinnati fire-escape and sustained injuries from which he died.

Henry Spillman was arrested in Springfield, O., on the charge of being a fugitive from justice, being an escaped convict from the Kentucky penitentiary.

In a reunion of the Stubbs family, near Elkton, Preble county, O., over three hundred relatives were present, representing eight different States.

Alfred Johnson, aged sixty years, Postmaster at Port William, O., who had been sick and despondent for some time, ended his misery by hanging himself.

At the picnic of the B. & O. employes, at Avondale, Licking Reservoir, O., Saturday, a colored man named Pearl, who struck a white man, was assaulted by the crowd and terribly beaten.

The Washington Park Club, of Chicago, offers $5,000 for a race between Miss Woodford and Freeland, or $6,000 between these two and Pontiac. Corsigan, owner of Freeland, will accept either proposition.

At Munice, Ind., Saturday morning, after a night of carousal, John Galbraith and Will Collina quarreled, and in an exchange of shots that followed Galbraith received a ball in his breast. He afterward accidentally shot himself in the leg.

At Wabpeton, Dakota, E. E. Redman's barn was struck by lightning, killing George Emery, and another man, name not known.

Two sailors, Martin Thompson, of Alpena, and Grant City, of Baffalo, both of the steam barge Araxas, were drowned in the river below Port Huron, Mich.

About forty thousand bushels No. 2 red winter wheat was posted, Saturday, at the New York Produce Exchange as out of condition in the Erie Basin stores.

Another case growing out of the assignment of Archbishop Purcell has been filed in the Ohio Supreme Court.

Ida Dingman, of Seymour, Ind., aged seventeen years, took a dose of Rough on Rats, and died.

A reduction of one cent per pound in the freight rate on hops from the Pacific coast to Eastern points has been made by all trans continental roads. The old rate was three cents. The new rate goes into effect September 2d.

B. F. Coates, of Portsmouth, Ohio, has been appointed receiver of the Cincinnati & Eastern road; vice John R. McLean, resigned.

Fire at Vincennes, Ind., at a late hour last night, did damage to the amount of $40,000.
At Portland, Oregon, Ira F. Powers' frame furniture factory was burned yesterday. Loss, $32,000; insurance, $18,000. An open wharf of the Oregonial Railway Company was damaged $10,000; not insured.

wallace-thompson-1885-08-26.A1:
GEORGIA AND FLORIDA.
THE NEWS OF THE TWO STATES
TOLD IN PARAGRAPHS.
A Cherokee County Lady Made Insane by Religious Excitement—An Alabama Driven from Home by Vigilant8 Seeks Refuge in Georgia—An Elbert County Negress Suspected of Murder.

GEORGIA.

Dr. Hazlehurst's residence at Brunswick was slightly damaged by lightning, Friday.

Revenue officers made a successful raid after moonshiners near Tallulah Falls Thursday night.

Joe Massey, at Marshallville, went out to his barn the other day, and with a stick killed 185 rats in an hour.

A Norwegian sailor named Peter Ellefser was fatally injured by falling from the masthead of the British bark Midas, at Brunswick, Friday.

A little son of E. G. Hodges had an arm broken, a day or two ago, by jumping from a moving train on the Columbus and Rome railroad at Forison.

At Buchanan, Robert M. Brown, charged with an attempt to assassinate J. T. Barnwell, has been sentenced to serve ten years in the penitentiary.

Prof. Maury stated in a report many years ago, that owing to Brunswick's peculiar geographical position, there would never be any serious harm done here by hurricane, cyclone or storm.

Mrs. William Thomas, of Cobb county, is visiting her sister, Mrs. S. J Baldwin, in Canton. She is accompanied by Mary Tallulah, a prodigy, who is 25 years old, and only about 30 inches high.

The City Light Guards, of Columbus, had a competitive drill among the members Thursday, for the gold badge awarded the company, at Macon, on July 4. It was won by Sergeant Fletcher Freeman.

A negress in Elbert county gave birth to a child a few days ago, which she carried off immediately and buried. It is not known whether the child was born alive or not. She has made threats that if it was born alive that it should not live. The affair will be investigated.

A few days ago Mrs. J. W. Maddox, of Wilkes county, found a silver thimble in the gizzard of a frying-sized chicken. The thimble was as bright as when it came from the jeweler. The chicken seemed to suffer no inconvenience, and was as game it had nothing but grit and plenty of
thmble was as bright as when it came from the jeweler. The chicken seemed to suffer no inconvenience, and was as game as if it had nothing but grit and plenty of it in its gizzard.

The only serious damage done at St. Simons by the gale on Monday night, was the sinking of the steamer Hamilton at the upper mill dock. Capt. Hotch now has her raised and on the beach near the basin gate. She is not injured as much as was at first supposed, and can be repaired at a moderate cost.

J. M. Kennedy, of Isabella, not contented with killing three coons with a stick one night recently while barefooted and in a briar patch, ran down and killed a possum whose tusks measured seventh of an inch from the edge of the gum. Mr. Kennedy drew the line, however, at a fox which was robbing his henroost. He said he would have caught it if it hadn't run in his high cotton.

Camilla correspondence News, Aug. 27. The caterpillars have cleaned up the cotton fields here. They have ruined the late cotton, and of course greatly cut off even the earliest planting. They have done more damage than in its ven years. Farmers have had only one good week for picking. The cotton all prematurely open is subject to rain and storms.—The big new hotel goes up with a rush.

As is well known, George W. Cheves, formerly editor of the Dawson Journal, is confined in the Atlanta jail for the killing of a man named Picket, in Dawson, several months ago. A few weeks since Dr. Boring, after a proper examination, stated that Mr. Cheves is now unquestionable. Mr. Cheves is now restored and in full possession of his mental faculties. He is a representative of one of the best Georgia families.

Thursday morning at 2 o'clock the gin-house of George N. Harris, five miles from Americus, was found to be on fire. By the most strenuous efforts, four bales of cotton were extinguished after being burned more or less. Two bales were burned for Mrs. Barwick, a widow lady, which Mr. Harris declares he will make good, although his own loss, in gin, press, buildings, cotton, cotton seed, etc., will not fall far short of $500. The fire was undoubtedly the work of an incendiary.

S. C. Hogan, of Cherokee county, has just taken his wife to the State lunatic asylum under sad circumstances. Mrs. Hogan is young and pretty. Her insanity was caused by religious excitement. Seven years ago she went to a camp-meeting and became so excited about religious matters that she lost her mind, and has never since fully recovered it. She has a fancy for bibles and religious papers, and steals them whenever possible. Mr. Hogan said that his wife was not averse to going to the asylum, as she had been there three times before, and imagines that Dr. Powell, the superintendent, is in love with her.

Wallace Thompson, a young man who resides about four miles from Columbus, in Lee county, Ala., was in Columbus, Friday, and reported that he was driven away from his home about midnight Wednesday night by a mob of masked men. They surrounded his home and broke open the door and window. He heard the beginning of the attack and made his escape by the back window in his night clothes. He says the mob pursued him a quarter of a mile, and then gave up the pursuit. He also states that they whipped several negroes on his place to force them to tell his whereabouts. The man has not been home since the attack. This is the second time a party has visited his house at night. He says that he sold all his possessions in Lee county, Friday, and never expects to cross the river into Alabama again. Thompson claims not to know the cause of the attacks. He says he knows the names of two of the party, and will disclose them.

STATE NEWS.
Gathered from Our Exchanges
Over the State.
Wholesale trade is picking up all over the State.

The next ex-Confederate reunion will be at Waco.

Tyler has incorporated a $10,000 canning company.

Planters in the vicinity of Calvert complain of boil worm.

To-day will be the great day of the Fort Worth reunion.

The Baptist State Sunday school convention is to meet at Brenham on the 20th instant.

Corsicana subscribes $50,000 to the Fort Worth, Sabine Pass and New Orleans narrow gauge.

A Laredo company will supply Texas cotton planters with Mexican laborers, on application.

Emile Turner, the little Waco waif, is dead. No clue to its parentage was ever received.

Crop reports from Troupe, Wharton, Marlin, Rockdale and Wharton are exceedingly favorable.

The District court at Austin will hold no session Saturday, out of respect to General Grant's memory.

The irrigation survey at Laredo demonstrates the possibility of extensive irrigation at small cost.

The maximum range of temperature throughout the State yesterday was from 90 to 98; minimum range 67 to 80.

Navasota is working up a waterworks boom. A $10,300 plant is offered, and the scheme will probably materialize.

El Paso is all alive over the municipal election, with 15 candidates for aldermen in the field, eight of them independents.

Only a small per cent of those attending Summer Normal schools applied for certificates, but of these a large per cent passed.

The printers on the Fort Worth Stock Journal left their cases Wednesday and Manager Hall supplied their places with non-union men.

Ten young Tylerites who have just reached their majority, have organized a newspaper company, and will issue their first sheet about the 15th instant.

The Mexican government is making strenuous efforts to stop smuggling across the Rio Grande below El Paso. Extra guards have been stationed in the passes.

The mysterious rattling of certain doors in Rockdale at unreasonable night hours has startled the whole town, and all attempts at solving the mystery have so far failed.

The mail carrier between Brady City and Camp San Sala is accused of tampering with the mails. His name is De Morrow, and he will be brought to Austin for examination.

Bryan, Brenham, Weimar, Seguin and Navasota have received their first bales of this year's cotton crop. Prices ranged from 10 to 12 cents; weight from 410 to 560 pounds per bale.

The General Assembly of K. of H. closed its sessions at Houston last night. Austin was selected as the next place of meeting. George R. Dashieil, of this city, was elected Grand Dictator.

The cattle men of Texas are interestedly awaiting the result of the President's peremptory order to the herders on the Indian lands to vacate. The extention of time for removal was denied at Washington.

Lynchburg will have a lynching bee on hand if the negro, one John Jones, who raped a white girl in that vicinity yesterday can be run down by the excited populace. His victim was found in an unconscious condition.

A dastardly attempt to burn Wills Point was made on last Wednesday night. The fire was discovered before it had made much progress, but was not put out until several thousand dollars worth of damage had been done. Many buildings were saturated with coal oil and full preparations made to clean out the business portion of town.

Austin escaped a general jail delivery yesterday afternoon by one of the escaping prisoners locking the door behind him as he passed out. Jailer Hornsly was overpowered as he was pouring water into the prisoners' cells and his pistol taken from him. Four prisoners escaped, all of whom were subsequently recaptured with the exception of Thomas Pearson, accused of murdering Dr. Stovall, who is still at large.

HOUSTON, Aug. 14.— [Special.] Wyatt Jones, a negro brute, who raped Miss Northcoutt, 16 years old, one week ago, near Lynchburg, in this county, and who escaped, was captured yesterday by negroes at Stafford Point and brought here to the sheriff and is now in jail. The people of Lynchburg have been hunting him ever since to lynch him. He denies the crime, but acknowledges to being the accused. The applications of Receiver M. G Howe to complete the Bromond road to connect with Suroveport will be granted to-morrow.
wyatt-jones-lynchburg-1885-08.A3:
Strapped to a Horse.
Houston, Aug., 18.
Wyatt Jones, the negro charged with raping Miss Norsecutt on the bank of the St. Jacinto River, near Lynchburg, was brought into the city at 2 o'clock this morning tied to a horse. He was in charge of two negro men, one of whom had captured Jones near Stafford's Point, twenty-five miles from Houston. Your correspondent interviewed him to-day. He claimed that he was innocent, but ran away because he feared lynching, owing to a suspicion resting on him that he had committed adultery. He has been fully identified as Wyatt Jones, the man who is charged with the crime. It is probable that Sheriff Fant will hold him here for examination, fearing that he will be lynched by the people at Lynchburg if sent there for examination.
